mcqs.question: Why does trial division for a single number n only need to check candidate divisors up to sqrt(n)?
options: Numbers above sqrt(n) are always prime themselves
Checking further would risk integer overflow on large n
Division becomes computationally more expensive past that point
If n had a divisor d greater than sqrt(n), then n/d would be a second divisor smaller than sqrt(n) — so any divisor above the root is mirrored by one below it
mcqs.explanation: Divisors of n always pair up as d and n/d, and if both exceeded sqrt(n) their product would exceed n — so if no divisor exists below sqrt(n), none exists above it either. That's a fact about factor pairs, not about primality of numbers past the root or division cost.

mcqs.question: What lets the Sieve of Eratosthenes beat calling a single-number primality test in a loop for all numbers up to N?
options: It marks every multiple of each found prime in bulk instead of independently re-deriving primality for each candidate
It uses a faster division algorithm internally than trial division does
It only checks odd numbers, cutting the work in half
It runs the same trial-division check but caches results in memory
mcqs.explanation: The sieve never divides anything to test a number — it strikes out multiples of each prime it discovers, so composites are eliminated in bulk rather than tested one at a time. That's a different algorithmic approach, not a faster division routine or a cache over the same per-number checks.

mcqs.question: In the Sieve of Eratosthenes, why does the inner marking loop for prime p start at p*p rather than 2*p?
options: Starting at p*p reduces the memory footprint of the boolean array
p*p is required to avoid marking p itself as composite
It's purely a stylistic convention with no effect on runtime
Every multiple of p below p*p already has a smaller prime factor and was struck out in an earlier pass, so starting there skips genuinely redundant work
mcqs.explanation: Any multiple of p smaller than p*p (like 2p, 3p, ..., (p-1)*p) has a prime factor smaller than p, and that smaller prime already marked it composite in an earlier pass — so starting at p*p avoids real, measurable redundant work, not just a style choice, and it doesn't touch memory usage at all.

mcqs.question: You need to check primality for a single number around 10^18, once. Which approach fits?
options: Build a full Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 10^18
A segmented sieve covering the full range up to that number
Trial division up to sqrt(n), or a probabilistic test like Miller-Rabin
Precompute a smallest-prime-factor table up to 10^18
mcqs.explanation: A sieve over 10^18 entries needs far more memory than exists, so both full and precomputed-table sieve approaches are physically impossible here; trial division (or Miller-Rabin for very large numbers) handles a single large check without needing to materialize the whole range.

mcqs.question: Why is it enough for a segmented sieve over the window [10^9, 10^9 + 10^6] to only use primes up to sqrt(10^9 + 10^6)?
options: Any composite number in the window must have a prime factor at or below sqrt of the window's upper bound, so smaller primes are sufficient to strike out every composite in it
Numbers above that square root are guaranteed prime by definition
The window is too small to contain any composite with a larger prime factor
It isn't actually enough — segmented sieves only approximate the correct prime list
mcqs.explanation: The same factor-pair fact from single-number trial division applies here: any composite has a factor at or below the square root of the bound, so sieving with only those small primes is guaranteed to catch every composite in the segment, regardless of window size or position.
